title: Climate indicators for Austria since 1961 at 1 km resolution
abstract: Climate indicators are essential for monitoring ongoing climate change, supporting climate impact research, conducting spatial hot spot analyses and assessing attribution questions. These efforts rely on high-quality, reliable datasets that adhere to FAIR data principles. We present a curated dataset of 117 climate indicators for Austria, covering the period from 1961 onward at a 1-km spatial resolution. The dataset includes climate indicators related to temperature, precipitation, radiation, snow, runoff and humidity, with spatial (area means) and temporal (climatological reference period means) aggregations to enable rapid climate impact analysis. The workflow used to compute these indices is supported by a careful technical validation procedure and is designed to ingest diverse climate datasets, enabling the creation of climate indices beyond the scope presented here. Both the dataset and the workflow thus offer a robust, flexible and user-friendly resource for advancing climate research and supporting informed decision-making.
problem: Existing climate indicator datasets often have limitations, such as a restricted number of indicators, coarse spatial resolutions, or a narrow focus, creating a gap in the availability of accessible, high-resolution, and well-curated data for robust climate analyses.
method: We present a reproducible workflow that uses quality-controlled daily meteorological data to compute a comprehensive, high-resolution dataset of 117 climate indicators for Austria since 1961, enabling detailed climate impact analyses.
task: The task is to present a curated, high-resolution (1 km) dataset of 117 climate indicators for Austria, covering the period from 1961 onward, to support climate monitoring and impact research.
innovation: This paper presents a comprehensive, quality-controlled dataset of 117 climate indicators for Austria from 1961 onward at a 1 km resolution, designed to facilitate robust climate impact analysis, monitoring, and informed decision-making.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: All input data are available at a daily resolution, spanning the time period from 1961-2025. The dataset covers Austria and its surrounding catchments, extending beyond national borders, and is provided in the ETRS89 / Austria Lambert projected coordinate system (EPSG:3416).

Set attributes: Output NetCDF data is stored with metadata attributes to ensure that the results are well-documented and self-descriptive. Metadata is structured in accordance with the CF Metadata Conventions, specifically adhering to CF-1.7 standards.

The climate indicators provided in this dataset are well-suited for studies investigating changes, trends, or dependencies in related climate impact phenomena. These encompass a wide range of areas, including natural hazards [27], forestry [28], public health [29], socio-ecologic systems, and economic impacts such as crop yields [30, 31].
[27] Schlögl, M., Fuchs, S., Scheidl, C. & Heiser, M. Trends in torrential flooding in the Austrian Alps: A combination of climate change, exposure dynamics, and mitigation measures. Climate Risk Management 32, 100294 (2021). https: //doi.org/10.1016/j.crm.2021.100294.

TGmean: The average daily mean temperature, calculated as: f(TG) = 1/n * sum(TGt) for t=1 to n
TNmean: The average daily minimum temperature, calculated as: f(TN) = 1/n * sum(TNt) for t=1 to n
TXmean: The average daily maximum temperature, calculated as: f(TX) = 1/n * sum(TXt) for t=1 to n
FD: The number of frost days, calculated as: f(TN) = sum of (1, if TNt < 0; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n
SU: The number of summer days, calculated as: f(TX) = sum of (1, if TXt > 25; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n
HD: The number of hot days, calculated as: f(TX) = sum of (1, if TXt > 30; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n
ID: The number of icing days, calculated as: f(TX) = sum of (1, if TXt < 0; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n
TR: The number of tropical nights, calculated as: f(TN) = sum of (1, if TNt > 20; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n

KYS: Kysely days are defined as the count of days in periods of at least 3 consecutive days where (1) TX ≥ 30 °C on the first day, (2) TX ≥ 25 °C on all subsequent days, and (3) and the average maximum temperature across all days in the period fulfills TX > 30 °C.
GSS: The day of the year corresponding to the first day of a four-day period during which TG > 5 °C on all days in the window.

GSL: The number of days between the start and end of the growing season. The growing season begins with a 6-day period where TG > 5 °C on all days in the window and ends with a 6-day period where TG < 5 °C on all days.
spring_backlash: The number of events counted as days where TNt < -2 °C for all days t after GSS and up to day 180 of the year. This is associated with spring frost.
SBI: The spring backlash index represents the growing degree days above 5 °C (see GDD5) for all days t occurring after GSS and up to the last spring backlash event.
TXx: The maximum daily maximum temperature, calculated as: f(TX) = max (TX)
TNx: The maximum daily minimum temperature, calculated as: f(TN) = max (TN)
TXn: The minimum daily maximum temperature, calculated as: f(TX) = min (TX)
TNn: The minimum daily minimum temperature, calculated as: f(TN) = min (TN)
TN10p: This indicator represents the percentage of days where the daily minimum temperature (TN) is below the 10th percentile (TN10p) of the reference period (1991-2020).
TX10p: Defined similarly to Equation 13, but with TX instead of TN
TN90p: Defined similarly to Equation 13, but with TNt > TN90p
TX90p: Defined similarly to Equation 13, but for TX instead of of TN and TXt > TX90p

WSDI: The warm spell duration index reflects the number of days within warm spells. Warm spells are defined as consecutive periods of at least 6 days where TX > TX90p. Here, TX90p is the 90th percentile of TX based on the reference period 1991-2020.

CSDI: The cold spell duration index reflects the number of days within cold spells. Cold spells are defined as consecutive periods of at least 6 days where TN < TN10p. Here, TN10p is the 10th percentile of TN based on the reference period 1991-2020.

BIO01: First bioclimatic indicator, representing the mean temperature calculated specifically for an annual aggregation period. It is equivalent to the general mean temperature as defined in Equation 1.
BIO02: The mean diurnal temperature range is calculated as the average difference between daily maximum temperature (TXt) and daily minimum temperature (TNt).
BIO03: The ratio of the mean diurnal temperature range (BIO02) and the annual temperature range (BIO07)
BIO04: Temperature seasonality is defined as the annual coefficient of variation in temperature, expressed as percentage
BIO05: The maximum daily maximum temperature (see Equation 9) for an annual aggregation period.
BIO06: The maximum daily maximum temperature (see Equation 12) for an annual aggregation period.
BIO07: The difference between the maximum daily maximum temperature (TXx) and the minimum daily minimum temperature (TNn). This is equivalent to Equation 20 for an annual aggregation period.
BIO10: The mean temperature for the warmest quarter, calculated as: f(TG) = 1/n * sum(TGj)
BIO11: The mean temperature for the coldest quarter, calculated as: f(TG) = 1/n * sum(TGj)
PRCPTOT: The total precipitation accumulated over a specified period, calculated as: f(RR) = sum(RRt) for t=1 to n
Rx1day: The maximum daily precipitation within a specified period, calculated as: f(RR) = max(RRt)
Rx5day: The maximum 5-day precipitation within a specified period, calculated as: f(RR) = max(RR5t)
SDII: The simple daily precipitation intensity index is defined as the average precipitation intensity on wet days, calculated as: f(RR) = 1/n_wet * sum(RRt,wet) for t=1 to n_wet
R10mm: The count of moderate wet days, calculated as: f(RR) = sum of (1, if RRt > c; 0, otherwise) for t=1 to n where c = 10 mm.
CDD: Consecutive dry days, defined as the number of days in the longest consecutive period where daily precipitation is less than 1 mm.
CWD: Consecutive wet days, defined as the number of days in the longest consecutive period where daily precipitation exceeds 1 mm.
R95pTOT: Similar to Equation 40, but for the 95th percentile.

BIO12: This indicator represents the total annual precipitation, calculated as the sum of daily precipitation totals over an entire year. It is equivalent to Equation 30, with the aggregation specifically applied to an annual time scale.
BIO13: The maximum daily precipitation within a year: f(RR) = max RRt
BIO14: The minimum daily precipitation within a year: f(RR) = min RRt
BIO15: The annual coefficient of variation of precipitation, expressed as a percentage: f(RR) = 100[%] * sigmaRR / muRR
BIO16: The total precipitation during the wettest season of the year, calculated as: f(RR) = sum(RRj)
BIO17: f(RR) = sum(RRj) where j is limited to the days inside the season where season = arg min(RRsea)
SAmean: The mean daily absolute sunshine duration over a specified period: f(SA) = 1/n * sum(SAt)
SRmean: The mean daily relative sunshine duration over a specified period: f(SR) = 1/n * sum(SRt)
ET0mean: The the average daily reference evapotranspiration over a specified period, calculated as: f(ET0) = 1/n * sum(ET0t)
HS_Q95: The 95th percentile of SDE.
NSD_72h: The maximum 3-day fresh snow depth ('new snow depth within 72 hours') within a specified period, calculated as: f(SF) = max(SF3t)

SHMI: The summer heat moisture index is defined as the ratio of the maximum monthly average temperature (TGmon) to the mean precipitation during summer months (June, July, August; RRJJA), calculated as: f(TG, RR) = max(TGmon) / RRJJA
BIO08: The mean temperature of the wettest quarter, calculated as: f(TG) = 1/n * sum(TGj)
BIO09: The mean temperature of the driest quarter, calculated as: f(TG) = 1/n * sum(TGj)
BIO18: The total precipitation during the warmest quarter, calculated as: f(RR) = sum(RRj)
BIO19: The total precipitation during the coldest quarter, calculated as: f(RR) = sum(RRj)
